question: In a typical clinic or hospital, about how much of the total waste generated is ordinary non-hazardous general rubbish?
explanation: You'd be surprised! The vast majority of waste coming from wards is just ordinary paper, food wrappings, and packaging—leaving only a small fraction that needs special hazardous care.

question: Why should you separate normal general waste from hazardous medical waste right from the start?

options.A: It ensures all waste can be recycled together safely.
options.B: It eliminates the need for any protective gear during disposal.
options.C: It reduces the volume of expensive hazardous waste treatment.
options.D: It allows general waste to be incinerated at high temperatures.

explanation: Treating medical waste safely is very costly. Keeping ordinary rubbish separate stops us from spending extra money and wasting precious resources on treating harmless items!

question: As a nurse, which group of bloodborne germs do you need to watch out for most when dealing with infectious waste?

options.A: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV

explanation: These three bloodborne viruses are our biggest worry in the ward because they are easily spread through accidental needle pricks and carry serious long-term health risks.

question: How do infectious germs from hospital waste most commonly find their way into a nurse's body?

options.A: Through accidental skin punctures or mucosal contact
options.B: Through breathing standard room air in patient wards
options.C: Through unbroken skin during routine ward cleaning
options.D: Through eating properly cooked hospital cafeteria food

explanation: Whenever there's a break in the skin (like a needle prick) or a splash into the eyes or mouth, germs in blood and body fluids get an open doorway straight into your body.

question: What is the main danger when handling genotoxic healthcare waste, such as cancer chemotherapy drugs?

options.C: Damage to cellular DNA and cancer risk

explanation: Genotoxic means 'toxic to genes.' These powerful drugs mess with cell DNA, which can cause mutations or cancer over time if we don't handle them with strict care.

question: A nurse accidentally drops and breaks an old mercury blood pressure machine on the ward floor. What kind of hazard is this?
explanation: Mercury is a toxic heavy metal, making it a chemical hazard. Its vapors can easily be breathed in or absorbed through the skin if not cleaned up properly!

question: Which common habit in the ward is a leading cause of accidental needle-prick injuries for nursing staff?

options.D: Placing sharps boxes at eye level

explanation: Never try to recap a used needle! Trying to guide that tiny cap back on with two hands is the number one way nurses accidentally jab their own fingers.

question: A nurse is accidentally poked by a needle from a patient who has Hepatitis B. Why is this exposure especially scary?

options.A: Hepatitis B spreads easily through casual air contact in the room.
options.B: There are no post-exposure vaccines or treatments available for Hepatitis B.
options.C: Hepatitis B has the highest transmission risk per exposure among common bloodborne viruses.
options.D: Hepatitis B can instantly destroy human skin cells on contact.

explanation: Compared to HIV or Hepatitis C, Hepatitis B is much more infectious. A single contaminated prick has a very high chance of passing the virus on if you aren't vaccinated.

question: What dangerous gases or chemicals are released when medical plastics and waste are burned in open drums?
explanation: Burning plastics at low temperatures (like in an open drum behind a clinic) creates nasty chemical pollutants called dioxins and furans, which poison the air we breathe.

question: A rural clinic throws its used syringes and needles into an open pit behind the building. What is the most likely danger to the community?

options.A: Contamination of local groundwater and accidental injuries to children
options.B: Reduction in the local population of disease vectors
options.C: Improved soil fertility for nearby farming
options.D: Purification of the surrounding air by medical chemicals

explanation: Open dumping is a serious safety threat. Exposed needles can easily injure playing children, and harmful chemicals or germs can wash down into drinking water wells.

question: At what exact moment in your daily clinical routine should you sort and segregate hospital waste?

options.C: At the exact point of generation

explanation: Always throw waste into the correct bin right where you use it! Sorting it immediately stops hazardous items from accidentally ending up in the general trash.

question: Why is it dangerous to stuff a sharps box until it is completely filled to the brim?

options.A: It increases the risk of needle stick injuries for anyone handling the box.
options.B: It makes the container too heavy to lift.
options.C: It prevents the waste from being incinerated properly.
options.D: It causes the plastic walls to dissolve chemically.

explanation: When a sharps box is overstuffed, needles poke out of the top. Anyone trying to close or carry the box risks getting painfully stuck!

question: Which Nigerian government agencies help set and enforce rules for environmental health and medical safety?

options.A: Ministry of Finance and Central Bank
options.C: Federal Ministry of Environment and NAFDAC

explanation: NAFDAC and the Federal Ministry of Environment work together to make sure healthcare facilities keep our environment safe and free from dangerous wastes.

question: As a student nurse, what is your main personal duty when it comes to hospital waste guidelines?

options.A: To prosecute scavengers who enter hospital grounds
options.B: To manufacture color-coded waste bags for the facility
options.C: To comply with disposal protocols and protect patients and staff from hazards
options.D: To design the hospital's waste incinerator plant

explanation: You are on the front lines! Following waste disposal rules every single day is one of the best ways you can keep your patients, your colleagues, and yourself safe.
